Title:
MEDICAL PHYSICSâ€“LED STRATIFIED DOSE OPTIMIZATION
 BENCHMARKS FOR DIGITAL BREAST TOMOSYNTHESIS: SUPPORTING
 MULTIDISCIPLINARY BREAST CARE
Authors: Nur Erina Ismail1, Nur Ashmira Aznan2, Zahurin Ismail1
Affiliations:
1 Hospital Putrajaya, Wilayah Persekutuan Putrajaya, Malaysia
 2 Medical Radiation Surveillance Division, Ministry of Health, Malaysia
Keywords:
Digital breast tomosynthesis; Medical physics; Dose optimization; Mean
 glandular dose; Quality improvement
Background:
High-quality breast imaging is essential for accurate diagnosis and multidisciplinary
 management of breast diseases. Clinical medical physicists play a key role in optimizing
 radiation dose while preserving diagnostic image quality. This study aimed to establish
 stratified dose optimization benchmarks based on acquisition projection and compressed
 breast thickness (CBT) for digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) to support patient safety
 and continuous quality improvement.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 A retrospective analysis of 200 DBT examinations acquired on a single mammography
 unit was performed. Examinations were stratified by projection (right and left
 craniocaudal [RCC/LCC] and mediolateral oblique [RMLO/LMLO]) and CBT. Mean
 glandular dose (MGD), tube voltage (kVp), tube currentâ€“time product (mAs), anode/filter
 combination, and CBT were recorded. Unlike national Diagnostic Reference Levels
 (DRLs), which are conventionally based on the 75th percentile, this study adopted the
 50th percentile MGD to establish facility-specific dose optimization benchmarks for
 continuous quality improvement while maintaining diagnostic image quality. Imaging
 system performance was verified using the IAEA-ATIA quality control software.
Results:
Results
 MGD increased with increasing CBT across all projections. MLO projections
 consistently demonstrated higher MGDs than CC projections, particularly in thicker
 breasts (LMLO â‰¥80 mm: 3.70 mGy versus LCC â‰¥70 mm: 2.97 mGy). Stratification by
 projection and CBT identified clinically relevant dose variations that would have been
 overlooked using a single institutional reference value. Quality control analysis
 confirmed stable and consistent imaging system performance throughout the study
 period.
Conclusion:
Projection- and CBT-specific dose optimization benchmarks provide a more
 individualized framework for radiation dose optimization in DBT than a single
 institutional reference level. Medical physics-led implementation of these stratified
 benchmarks supports continuous quality improvement, balances radiation dose with
 diagnostic image quality, and facilitates accurate diagnosis and multidisciplinary clinical
 decision-making in breast disease management.

Title:
BILATERAL SYNCHRONOUS DUCTAL
 CARCINOMA IN SITU DETECTED ON BREAST
 MRI FOLLOWING IMAGINGâ€“PATHOLOGY
 DISCORDANCE
Authors: Raja Ellysya1, Ani Anisa2
Affiliations:
1Department of Radiology, Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz UKM , Kuala Lumpur,
 Malaysia
Keywords:
Ductal carcinoma in situ; Breast MRI; Non-mass enhancement; Imaging-
 pathology discordance; Bilateral synchronous disease
Background:
Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) commonly presents as suspicious microcalcifications on
 mammography. However, some lesions present as non-mass enhancement (NME) on breast
 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which may be occult or underestimated on conventional
 imaging. MRI is valuable in evaluating disease extent and identifying additional lesions,
 particularly when imaging findings do not correlate with pathology. We report a case in
 which MRI detected occult bilateral synchronous DCIS, resulting in a significant change in
 surgical management.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 43-year-old woman presented with spontaneous left nipple discharge and a palpable left
 breast lump. Initial mammography and ultrasound demonstrated a BI-RADS 3 lesion, and
 ultrasound-guided biopsy confirmed intermediate-grade DCIS. She underwent wide local
 excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy followed by re-excision because of involved and
 close surgical margins. Histopathology subsequently demonstrated persistent intermediate- to
 high-grade DCIS associated with an intraductal papilloma.
 Despite repeated surgery, the extent of disease remained discordant with conventional
 imaging findings. Breast MRI demonstrated bilateral suspicious outer quadrant non-mass
 enhancement. Targeted ultrasound-guided biopsies confirmed bilateral ER-positive DCIS,
 with intraductal papilloma containing intermediate-grade DCIS in the right breast and
 intermediate- to high-grade DCIS with adenosis in the left breast. Based on these findings,
 the planned repeat breast-conserving surgery was changed to bilateral skin-sparing
 mastectomy with immediate implant reconstruction.
Results:
Discussion
 This case highlights the importance of breast MRI as a problem-solving modality in patients
 with imaging-pathology discordance. MRI identified occult synchronous contralateral disease
 that was not confidently demonstrated on conventional imaging, allowing more accurate
 assessment of disease extent and appropriate surgical planning. Recognition of suspicious
 NME is essential, particularly in patients with persistent or recurrent DCIS.
Conclusion:
Breast MRI plays a pivotal role in evaluating imaging-pathology discordance, detecting
 occult bilateral synchronous DCIS, and guiding multidisciplinary treatment planning.
 Recognition of suspicious non-mass enhancement can significantly influence surgical
 management and improve patient care.

Title:
PRIMARY NEUROENDOCRINE CARCINOMA OF THE BREAST: A MULTIDISCIPLINARY
 DIAGNOSTIC AND THERAPEUTIC CHALLENGE
Authors: Dr. Ng Hui Rou, Co-AuthorÂ¹: Dr. Farhana Binti Fadzli
Affiliations: Department of Biomedical Imaging, University Malaya Medical Centre, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Keywords:
Neuroendocrine carcinoma; Breast cancer; Breast imaging; Nuclear medicine; Multidisciplinary
 management
Background:
Primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the breast is a rare malignancy with non-specific imaging features and no
 established treatment pathway. Accurate diagnosis and management require close collaboration between breast
 radiology, nuclear medicine, pathology, surgery and oncology.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 54-year-old woman presented with a progressively enlarging right breast lump and 10 kg weight loss over
 three months. Mammography demonstrated an ill-defined hyperdense mass without suspicious calcifications.
 Ultrasound showed an irregular vascular hypoechoic 25 mm mass at the 12 o'clock position (BI-RADS 5). Core
 biopsy demonstrated invasive carcinoma with neuroendocrine differentiation, showing diffuse synaptophysin
 positivity, estrogen receptor positivity, HER2 negativity and a Ki-67 index of approximately 40%. FDG PET-
 CT performed by the nuclear medicine team demonstrated metabolically active disease confined to the breast
 without regional or distant metastases, supporting curative treatment. The patient underwent right mastectomy
 with sentinel lymph node biopsy. Histopathology confirmed a 3.2 cm grade 3 invasive neuroendocrine
 carcinoma with associated ductal carcinoma in situ. One sentinel lymph node contained metastatic carcinoma
 with extranodal extension and the deep margin was involved. Completion axillary dissection revealed no
 additional nodal metastases. Following multidisciplinary team discussion, the patient received platinum-
 etoposide chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy.
Results:
Discussion
 This case highlights the complementary roles of breast radiology in lesion detection and biopsy guidance,
 pathology in confirming neuroendocrine differentiation, nuclear medicine in excluding occult metastatic
 disease, and the multidisciplinary breast team in integrating these findings to formulate individualized
 treatment.
Conclusion:
Successful management of primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the breast relies on multidisciplinary
 collaboration for accurate diagnosis, comprehensive staging and personalized treatment of this rare breast
 malignancy.

Title:
BREAST CANCER OBSCURED BY COSMETIC BREAST FILLER INJECTIONS:
 DIAGNOSTIC CHALLENGES AND IMAGING PITFALLS IN TWO CASES
Authors: Ernisha SaibÂ¹, Nazimah Ab MuminÂ¹, Marlina Tanty Ramli HamidÂ¹, Nor Faezan Abdul Rashid 2
Affiliations:
1 Department of Radiology, Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Teknologi MARA, Sungai Buloh,
 Selangor, Malaysia.
 2 Department of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, Universiti Teknologi MARA, Sungai Buloh,
 Selangor, Malaysia.
Keywords: breast cancer, breast imaging, breast filler injection, diagnostic pitfall.
Background:
Cosmetic breast filler injections may produce extensive inflammatory, fibrotic and nodular
 changes that both mimic malignancy and obscure breast parenchyma, creating diagnostic
 challenges in breast cancer detection and staging.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 We report two patients with previous breast filler injections who subsequently presented with
 suspicious breast findings. Case 1: Screening mammography and ultrasound demonstrated a
 suspicious left breast lesion with ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy against a background
 of diffuse filler-related changes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) further characterized the
 abnormality, and image-guided biopsy confirmed invasive carcinoma. Case 2: A patient with
 a palpable breast abnormality underwent MRI because conventional imaging was
 inconclusive in the presence of extensive filler-related changes. MRI demonstrated a
 suspicious enhancing lesion, and biopsy revealed invasive carcinoma with associated ductal
 carcinoma in situ.
Results:
Discussion
 Breast filler material may conceal or simulate lesions on mammography and ultrasound and
 can hinder identification of a reliable sonographic target for biopsy. These cases demonstrate
 the value of multimodality assessment, particularly contrast-enhanced MRI, when
 conventional imaging findings are inconclusive. Where a lesion lacks a reliable sonographic
 correlate, an alternative image-guided biopsy approach may be required. Multidisciplinary
 review is important for selecting the appropriate imaging and biopsy strategy and for defining
 disease extent.
Conclusion:
A history of cosmetic breast filler injection should be actively sought in women undergoing
 breast assessment. Early escalation to contrast-enhanced imaging and a tailored biopsy
 strategy may reduce diagnostic delay and facilitate accurate staging and management when
 mammographic or sonographic evaluation is limited.

Title:
BREAST BIOPSIES ARE NOT DONE LIGHTLY: A RETROSPECTIVE REVIEW
 OF 1307 BREAST BIOPSIESâ€
Authors:
Ying Ying Ooi 1 , Farhana Fadzli 2 , Harjit Kaur 1 , Normayah Kitan 1 , Bang Rom Lee 3 , Char Hong
 Ng 1 , Cheng Har Yip 1 , Maninderpal Kaur 2
Affiliations:
Department of Breast Surgery, Picaso Hospital, Petaling Jaya, Malaysia
 2 Department of Breast Imaging, Picaso Hospital, Petaling Jaya, Malaysia
 3 Department of Anatomical Pathology, Picaso Hospital, Petaling Jaya, Malaysia
Keywords:
Breast biopsy, BI-RADS classification, Diagnostic yield, Histopathological
 diagnosis, Positive Predictive Value 2 (PPV2)
Background:
This report evaluates the diagnostic yield of imaging-guided and palpation-guided breast
 biopsies in Picaso Hospital from October 2024 to June 2026. The primary aim is to evaluate
 the overall positive predictive value 2 (PPV2) of breast biopsies performed.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 A retrospective study was conducted on 1212 patients who had undergone imaging-guided or
 clinically-guided breast biopsies in Picaso Hospital from October 2024 to June 2026. 1307
 biopsies were performed. Variables like age, BI-RADS category, and histopathological
 diagnosis, were collected and used for analysis. The PPV2 overall and of each BI-RADS
 category were calculated and compared with ACR benchmarks.
Results:
Results
 A total of 1307 samples of diagnostic biopsies with confirmed histopathology were analysed.
 BI-RADS 4 constituted the largest proportion of biopsies taken, being 59% (n=715), followed
 by BI-RADS 5 at 32% (n=387). BI-RADS 3 lesions comprised 7.2% (n=87) of all biopsies.
 BI-RADS 1 and 2 accounted for 0.2% (n=3) and 1.6% (n=19) respectively.
 This study yielded an overall PPV2 of 48.6%, exceeding the ACR benchmark of â‰¥25%.
 40.9% (n=534) biopsies were benign; 10.6% (n=138) were borderline lesions requiring
 subsequent active management.
 PPV2 was 21.05% for BI-RADS 2, 10.34% for BI-RADS 3, 31.89% for BI-RADS 4, and
 88.89% for BI-RADS 5. Both BI-RADS 4 and 5 exceeded the ACR benchmark.
Conclusion:
In conclusion, the breast biopsies performed in Picaso Hospital yielded a high overall
 diagnostic yield of almost 50%, suggesting appropriate integration of clinical judgement with
 imaging findings in guiding patient selection for biopsies. In some exceptions, BI-RADS 2
 lesions were biopsied due to clinical suspicion, resulting in a non-zero PPV2. Opportunities
 for further optimisation include close monitoring of borderline lesions outcomes to determine
 the upgrade rate to malignancy.

Title:
THE POWER TO PRESS: EVALUATING PAIN, DOSE, AND IMAGE QUALITY
 IN PATIENT-LED MAMMOGRAPHY
Authors:
Raihanah Haroon 1 , Sivaneswary A/P Muniappan 1 , Siti Kamariah Che Mohamed 1 ,
 Karimah Hanim Abd. Aziz 2 , Nor Ain Rabaiee 1 , Intan Bazilah Abu Bakar
Affiliations:
Â¹ Department of Radiology, Kulliyyah of Medicine, International Islamic University
 Malaysia
 2 Department of Community Medicine, Kulliyyah of Medicine, International Islamic
 University Malaysia
Keywords: self-assisted compression, mammography, pain experience
Background:
Mammography is the gold standard for early breast cancer detection, but compression-
 associated pain severely hinders screening adherence. Self-assisted compression offers a
 patient-centered approach to improve this experience. This quasi-experimental study
 evaluated the effectiveness of self-assisted versus conventional mammographer-assisted
 compression regarding mammographic pain, radiation dose, and image quality at Sultan
 Ahmad Shah Medical Centre (SASMEC @IIUM).
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 A total of 412 participants were enrolled (mammographer-assisted, n = 210; supervised
 self-assisted, n = 202). Pain intensity was categorized (none, mild, moderate, severe),
 radiation dose was evaluated using Mean Glandular Dose (MGD), and image quality was
 graded via standardized Perfect-Good-Moderate-Inadequate (PGMI) criteria. Data were
 analyzed using Chi-square tests, Mannâ€“Whitney U tests, multinomial logistic regression,
 and multiple linear regression to determine independent predictors of outcomes.
Results:
Results
 The majority of participants experienced only mild pain (71%), with no statistically
 significant difference in pain intensity between the two techniques (p = 0.308).
 Multinomial logistic regression confirmed that compression technique was not a
 significant predictor of pain. Similarly, no significant differences were observed in
 compressed breast thickness or MGD for both CC and MLO views (p < 0.05), indicating
 comparable dose optimization. While image quality showed a significant association with
 technique (p = 0.024) due to a technical advantage in the mammographer-assisted group,
  self-assisted compression consistently achieved predominantly moderate-to-good quality,
 ensuring full diagnostic adequacy. Instead of compression technique, sociodemographic
 factors independently predicted outcomes. Ethnicity and education predicted pain, while
 age, ethnicity, and education predicted breast thickness and MGD.
Conclusion:
Self-assisted compression is a highly feasible, clinically safe, and patient-centered
 alternative to standard mammography. It yields equivalent pain outcomes and radiation
 doses while maintaining acceptable diagnostic image quality. Patient-centered
 mammographic care must account for sociodemographic variations, which influence the
 screening experience more heavily than the physical mode of compression control.

Title:
PERMANENT OR TEMPORARY? INSIGHTS FROM A SINGLE-INSTITUTION
 SURVEY OF SINGAPORE WOMEN'S PREFERENCE FOR BREAST BIOPSY
 MARKER TYPES
Authors: Stefanie Lee 1 , Tan Si Ying 2 , Iris Neo 3 , Lester Leong 3
Affiliations:
1 Department of Diagnostic Radiology, Singapore General Hospital, Singaporef
 2 Department of Breast Surgery, Singapore General Hospital, Singapore
 3 Department of Diagnostic Radiology, Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, Singapore
Keywords: Breast, Biopsy, Clip, Metallic, Biodegradable
Background:
Metallic clips are commonly deployed after breast biopsies for lesional localization. Because
 they are retained indefinitely, some women experience foreign-body anxiety, occasionally
 leading to procedure refusal. We evaluated womenâ€™s attitudes toward permanent metallic clips
 and the acceptability of hypothetical biodegradable alternatives.
Materials & Methods:
Methods:
 Following IRB approval, a prospective survey at a single Singapore institution recruited women
 aged >21 years across three cohorts: (1) patients undergoing breast needle biopsy requiring clips,
 (2) women with previous clip insertion, and (3) female breast care physicians (surgeons,
 radiologists, pathologists). Participants were surveyed on demographics, clip preferences
 (permanent metallic vs. biodegradable), and underlying reasons.
Results:
Results:
 Between 2015 and 2024, 162 women were surveyed: 71 undergoing biopsy (43.8%), 73 with
 prior clip placement (45.1%), and 18 doctors (11.1%). Overall, 56.2% (91/162) preferred
 biodegradable clips, 21.6% (35/162) preferred permanent metallic clips, and 21.6% (35/162) had
 no preference. Strikingly, 27.8% of the female doctors preferred a biodegradable clip despite
 their medical background, although women in the combined breast biopsy group were still
 significantly more likely to prefer biodegradable clips (59.7%) than doctors (p=0.012). Women
 undergoing biopsy were also more likely than those with existing clips to prefer biodegradable
 clips (73.2% vs. 46.6%, p=0.001). Key motivators included psychological unease with having a
 permanent foreign body in the breast (84.6%), followed by concerns about the potential long-
 term effects of metallic clips (12.1%). Additionally, 76% of neutral respondents were still open
 to biodegradable clips.
Conclusion:
Women's concerns regarding permanent metallic clips deserve greater recognition rather than
 assuming they are universally tolerated. Our findings identify a potential unmet need for
 biodegradable biopsy markers - greater investment into developing safe biodegradable
 alternatives to improve patient acceptance and enhance the overall breast biopsy experience is
 needed.

Title:
RECURRENT HEMORRHAGIC GIANT CYSTIC INVASIVE BREAST
 CARCINOMA SUCCESSFULLY MANAGED WITH PREOPERATIVE
 TRANSARTERIAL EMBOLIZATION: A RARE CASE REPORT
Authors: 1 Harun Fathinah, 1 Basir Ani Anisa
Affiliations:
Department of Radiology, Hospital Canselor Tuanku Muhriz, Jalan Yaacob Latif, Bandar
 Tun Razak Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Keywords:
Invasive breast carcinoma, no special type, Haemorrhagic complex cystic breast
 lesion, Transarterial embolization
Background:
Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (IBC-NST) typically presents as a solid breast
 mass. Presentation as a giant haemorrhagic cystic lesion is extremely uncommon and may
 mimic a benign complex breast cyst. Although transarterial embolization has been described
 for haemorrhage from ulcerating or locally advanced breast cancers, its application for
 recurrent intralesional bleeding within a cystic invasive carcinoma has rarely been reported.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 71-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with a progressively enlarging painless right
 breast mass of one year's duration. Ultrasonography demonstrated a large mixed solid-cystic
 breast lesion with a vascular mural solid component. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded
 1,650 mL of dark hemorrhagic fluid, followed by core biopsy of the solid component, which
 confirmed grade 3 invasive breast carcinoma of no special type. Despite repeated aspiration,
 rapid reaccumulation of hemorrhagic fluid suggested ongoing bleeding from the vascular
 tumour component. Transarterial embolization of multiple tumour-feeding arteries was
 performed, achieving near stasis. The patient subsequently received neoadjuvant
 chemotherapy followed by right mastectomy with axillary dissection. Adjuvant radiotherapy
 was completed, with planned capecitabine therapy.
Results:
Discussion
 Haemorrhagic cystic presentation of invasive breast carcinoma is exceedingly rare. Bloody or
 dark hemoserous aspirate from a breast cyst, particularly in the presence of a vascular mural
 nodule, should prompt suspicion for malignancy and immediate tissue diagnosis. This case
 highlights the rare presentation of invasive breast carcinoma and demonstrates that
 transarterial embolization may provide effective control of recurrent tumour-related
 intralesional bleeding, facilitating subsequent oncological treatment and definitive surgery.
Conclusion:
This case illustrates a rare presentation of invasive breast carcinoma as a giant haemorrhagic
 cystic breast lesion with recurrent intralesional bleeding. Persistent haemorrhagic
 reaccumulation after aspiration should raise concern for malignancy. Preoperative
 transarterial embolization may represent a valuable adjunctive treatment for controlling
 tumour-related bleeding, allowing safe administration of neoadjuvant therapy and subsequent
 definitive surgical management.

Title:
WHEN SOFT DOES NOT MEAN BENIGN: LIMITATIONS OF ULTRASOUND
 ELASTOGRAPHY IN MUCINOUS BREAST CARCINOMA - A COHORT
 STUDY WITH RADIOLOGICâ€“PATHOLOGIC CORRELATION
Authors:
Benjamin Livingston Farah 1 (presenting author), Leong Chee Hao Lester 2 , Sushmita
 Chandran 2 , Tan Si Ying
Affiliations:
1. Department of Anatomical Pathology, Singapore General Hospital, Singapore
 2. Department of Diagnostic Radiology, Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, Singapore
 3. Department of Breast Surgery, Singapore General Hospital, Singapore
 4. Department of Breast Surgery, National Cancer Centre Singapore, Singapore
 5. SingHealth Duke-NUS Breast Centre, Singapore
Keywords: Elastography, Mucinous Breast Carcinoma, Absent Desmoplasia
Background:
Breast strain elastography improves differentiation of benign and malignant breast
 masses by assessing tissue stiffness, as most invasive carcinomas are stiff and induce a
 surrounding desmoplastic reaction, resulting in an enlarged elastographic size ratio
 (ESR). Mucinous breast carcinoma (MBC), however, is characterised by abundant
 extracellular mucin and minimal desmoplastic response, potentially producing a soft and
 benign elastographic appearance. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of
 strain elastography in MBC and investigated histopathological factors associated with
 false-negative elastographic findings.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 In this retrospective study, histologically confirmed MBCs diagnosed between 2000 and
 2020 were identified from a multi-institutional joint breast cancer registry. Ninety cases
 with preoperative ultrasound strain elastography were analysed. Quantitative ESR was
 assessed using a threshold of >;1.1 as suspicious, while qualitative strain patterns were
 classified as hard or soft/intermediate. Imaging findings were correlated with
 histopathological subtype (pure versus mixed mucinous carcinoma) and the presence of a
 desmoplastic reaction.
Results:
Results
 Using an ESR threshold of >;1.1, only 60.0% (54/90) of MBCs were classified as
 suspicious, whereas 40.0% (36/90) demonstrated benign ESRs, indicating reduced
 sensitivity of strain elastography in this tumour subtype. Mixed mucinous carcinomas
 were significantly more likely than pure mucinous carcinomas to demonstrate suspicious
 ESRs (90.0% vs 56.3%, p=0.046), corresponding to a greater propensity for desmoplastic
 reaction on histopathology. Qualitative strain assessment showed stiff internal strain
 patterns in 74.4% (67/90) of lesions, with no significant difference between mixed and
 pure mucinous carcinomas (60.0% vs 76.3%, p=0.270).
Conclusion:
MBC is an important cause of false-negative strain elastography, particularly the pure
 subtype, owing to its lack of desmoplastic reaction and absence of an enlarged
 elastographic size ratio. Recognition of this diagnostic pitfall and correlation with
 conventional ultrasound findings are essential to avoid misdiagnosis.

Title: RADIO SILENCE: A CASE-BASED DISCUSSION ON TROUBLESHOOTING SAVI SCOUTÂ® NON-DETECTION OF INTRAOPERATIVE REFLECTOR SIGNAL
Authors: Tan NingÂ¹ (Presenter), Clement Chia Luck KhngÂ², Chuang Xue En2, Zoe Lim Soon Yee2, Lily Lai Mei San1, Lester Leong Chee Hao1
Affiliations:
Department of Diagnostic Radiology, Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, Singapore
 2 Department of General Surgery, Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, Singapore
Keywords: Savi Scout, Signal Non-Detection, Wire-Free Localisation
Background:
The SAVI SCOUT® radar localisation system is an increasingly adopted wire-free technology for preoperative localisation of breast lesions. Although highly reliable, rare instances of failure to detect signal from the reflector can occur, which can potentially lead to surgical failure. Because such cases are seldom reported, practical troubleshooting guidance remains limited.
 We present a challenging case of intraoperative failure to detect SAVI SCOUT® signal and suggest potential troubleshooting solutions.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 54-year-old woman with newly diagnosed breast cancer underwent ultrasound-guided placement of a SAVI SCOUT® reflector one week before surgery to localise a 5mm malignant satellite mass at the posterior 10 o'clock position of the right breast, located 2.5 cm deep to the skin. Although an intermittent reflector signal was detected immediately after deployment, no signal could be identified intraoperatively. 
 After several unsuccessful attempts to detect the reflector, intraoperative ultrasound was eventually able to identify its location, albeit with some difficulty. After the initial breast incision and elevation of the skin flap, the SAVI SCOUTÂ® probe successfully detected the reflector signal, allowing successful excision of both the lesion and reflector.
Results:
Discussion
 We discuss various possible solutions to troubleshooting intraoperative signal failure, including optimisation of SAVI SCOUT® probe orientation, repositioning or flattening of the breast, use of intraoperative ultrasound and utility of fluoroscopy.
Conclusion: This case illustrates the rare but important problem of intraoperative failure to detect the SAVI SCOUT® reflector signal and raises awareness of possible practical solutions and adjunct localisation techniques to facilitate successful lesion excision.

Title:
"SEEING FASTER, SEEING SHARPER" - QUANTITATIVE INTER-READER
 COMPARISON OF ULTRAFAST VERSUS STANDARD DYNAMIC
 CONTRAST-ENHANCED BREAST MRI
Authors:
Pik Hey Lee 1 , Pak Lun Lam 1 , Cherry Cheuk Yan Chan 1 , Wai Pan Cheung 1 , Lai Wan Lo 1 ,
 Wing Sze Mak 1 , Lily Ka Man Wong 1 , Eliza Po Yan Eliza Fung 1
Affiliations:
Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology, Kwong Wah Hospital, Hong
 Kong SAR
Keywords: Breast Neoplasm, Dynamic Contrast Enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Background:
Ultrafast dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI is a high temporal resolution technique
 for breast lesion characterisation, though its potential to improve lesion conspicuity
 remains debated. This study aims to perform quantitative inter-reader comparison of
 enhancing breast lesion conspicuity in ultrafast versus standard DCE MRI.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 This single-centre retrospective study reviewed consecutive breast MRI performed from
 March 2024 to March 2025 with pathologically proven breast lesions. Ultrafast and
 standard DCE sequences were performed in the same session. These studies were divided
 into two sets, each containing either ultrafast or standard DCE MRI, in randomised order.
 Two breast radiologists independently assessed the two sets in a blinded fashion, with a
 three-month washout period. Enhancing breast lesions and breast parenchyma were
 segmented manually to calculate contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) for quantitative
 conspicuity assessment. Each study was also assessed for image quality on a five-point
 Likert scale. Background parenchymal enhancement (BPE), lesion morphology and
 enhancement pattern were evaluated according to BI-RADS v2025. Comparisons were
 made using Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Inter-rater agreement was performed using
 Cohen's kappa.
Results:
Results
 A total of 71 studies (median age 60.1 years) with 95 enhancing breast lesions (49
 benign, 46 malignant) were assessed. Overall, CNR breast lesions were higher on
 ultrafast than standard DCE MRI (23.4 vs 21.2, p=0.002). In subgroup analysis, this
 difference remained significant in patients with moderate or marked BPE (26.7 vs 22.4,
 p=0.002) and in malignant lesions (22.8 vs 17.7, p<0.001), but not in patients with
 minimal or mild BPE (21.0 vs 21.1, p=0.272) or in benign lesions (25.3 vs 24.9,
 p=0.214). While image quality was inferior in ultrafast studies (4 vs 5, p<0.001), inter-
 rater agreement on lesion morphology and enhancement pattern remained high (K>0.90).
Conclusion:
Ultrafast DCE MRI improves conspicuity of breast lesions, especially for patients with
 moderate or high BPE, and in malignancy.

Title:
EARLY BREAST CANCER DETECTION USING COMPLEMENTARY
 MULTIMODALITY IMAGING FROM CONVENTIONAL TO ADVANCE TO
 ACHIEVED BETTER PROGNOSIS.
Authors:
Yashinta G., Maria Angelina1
 
 , Choridah, Lina2
 
 , Hikmawati, Sariningsih3
Affiliations:
1Tzu Chi Hospital, Jakarta, Indonesia, 2Radiology Department, Faculty of Medicine, Public Health,
 and Nursing Gadjah Mada University, Yogyakarta, Indonesia, 3 Dharmais Cancer Center Hospital,
 Jakarta, Indonesia.v
Keywords: multimodality imaging, breast ultrasound, DBT, Breast MRI, early diagnosis.
Background:
Finding of small suspicious non palpable lesions in patient with atypical symptom often become a
 diagnostic challenge. Multimodality imaging is needed to help establish the diagnosis before patient
 undergoing invasive procedures. Correct diagnosis of small lesions ensures a good prognosis.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 64-year-old female patient presented with left shoulder pain. Breast ultrasound was performed
 to rule out pathology, chosen because mammography is not available in the first hospital. It revealed
 a small, non-palpable, irregular, suspicious lesion at 2 o'clock, 5 cm from the left nipple, measuring
 4.7 mm. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) in the other hospital showed heterogeneous breast
 composition, without focal asymmetry or architectural distortion. Contrast-enhanced breast MRI
 revealed an enhanced, irregular lesion with indistinct margins measuring 7.4 mm with type I kinetic
 curve, low suspicion for malignancy (BI-RADS 4A). Patient refused biopsy or lumpectomy
 recommended by the oncologist. A 6-month ultrasound follow-up revealed an enlarged lesion with
 one new suspicious nodule. Breast-conserving surgery was performed, but the incision margins
 were not tumor-free, leading to a modified mastectomy. Pathology revealed a grade 3 multifocal
 invasive carcinoma of no-special-type with DCIS without axillary lymph node involvement. Post-
 mastectomy PET scan showed no axillary lymph node spread or distant metastases.
Results:
Discussion
 Detecting breast carcinoma at early stage with mammography and breast ultrasound is crucial for
 ensuring good clinical outcome. Mammography in dense breasts may be low sensitive for detecting
 masses, but can assess the presence of microcalcification or architectural distortion. In early breast
 cancer with small lesions, if mammography and ultrasound are inconclusive, MRI is required to
 help confirm the diagnosis before invasive procedures. Post-contrast enhancement on breast MRI can detect lesions not visible on mammography.
Conclusion:
Multimodality imaging (ultrasound, mammography/DBT, Breast MRI) is needed for the
 management of patients with early breast cancer to achieve a good prognostic outcome.

Title: CHRONIC SUPPURATIVE MASTITIS MIMICKING BREAST CANCER IN A NON-PUERPERAL WOMAN: A CASE REPORT
Authors: S. Hayuningsih 1 , T. W. Handarini 2 , L. Choridah
Affiliations:
1 Fellowship student of Woman Imaging
 2 Soetomo Academic General Hospital
 
 3 Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing UGM/ Dr. Sardjito General Hospital
 Prof. Dr. W. Z. Johannes Regional General Hospital, Kupang, East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia
Keywords:
chronic suppurative mastitis, breast cancer, histopathological examination, non
 puerperal.
Background:
Introduction: Chronic suppurative mastitis is a rare benign inflammatory breast disease
 characterized by persistent infection, chronic inflammation, and abscess formation. It is clinical
 and radiological features may closely mimic breast carcinoma, making histopathological
 examination essential for definitive diagnosis.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation: A 23 year old non puerperal woman with no history of breastfeeding
 presented with a one-month history of painful swelling and mild erythema of the left breast,
 referred from Oncologist Surgeon, as suspected Malignancy. Breast ultrasonography
 demonstrated an irregular hypoechoic mass, wider than taller, with echogenic material, without
 internal moving echo, accompanied by soft tissue edema and suspicious left axillary
 lymphadenopathy, raising concern for breast malignancy. Chest radiography revealed a left
 breast soft tissue mass without pulmonary abnormalities. However, histopathological
 examination confirmed chronic suppurative mastitis without evidence of tuberculosis and
 malignancy.
Results:
Discussion: This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of chronic suppurative mastitis in a
 non puerperal young woman. Imaging findings, including irregular hypoechoic mass, wider than
 taller, with echogenic material, without internal moving echo, accompanied by soft tissue edema,
 and with axillary lymphadenopathy, may overlap substantially with those of breast cancer,

Conclusion: Chronic suppurative mastitis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of

Background:

 demonstrate overlapping clinical, imaging, and histopathological features, making preoperative
 diagnosis challenging. Although ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) is the standard
 method for tissue diagnosis, sampling limitations in large heterogeneous lesions may result in
 radiologic-pathologic discordance. We report a giant fibroepithelial breast lesion highlighting the
 importance of imaging-pathology correlation.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation.

 five years. Breast ultrasonography demonstrated a giant multilobulated hypoechoic solid mass
 with circumscribed margins, non-parallel orientation, and increased intra- and perilesional
 vascularity on color Doppler, occupying the lower outer quadrant of the right breast. The lesion
 measured >7 cm and exceeded the ultrasound field of view, limiting posterior chest wall
 evaluation. Additional bilateral fibroadenoma-like nodules and multiple simple cysts were
 identified. No suspicious axillary lymphadenopathy was detected. The dominant lesion was
 categorized as BI-RADS 4A, suggesting a giant fibroepithelial lesion with differential diagnoses
 of giant fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor. Ultrasound-guided CNB revealed fibroadenoma with
 myxoid stromal degeneration and stromal hyalinization without malignancy. Because the benign
 pathology was discordant with the suspicious imaging findings, the patient was referred to the
 National Cancer Center Dharmais for definitive surgical management. Final surgical
 histopathology was pending at the time of abstract submission.

Discussion
 Giant fibroadenomas and phyllodes tumors share overlapping sonographic features, including
 large size, multilobulated contour, heterogeneous echotexture, and increased vascularity.
 Sampling error on CNB may underestimate phyllodes tumor in large heterogeneous lesions.
 Therefore, radiologic-pathologic correlation and multidisciplinary assessment are essential when
 discordance is encountered.
Conclusion:
Radiologic-pathologic discordance should prompt further evaluation despite benign CNB
 findings. Triple assessment remains essential for appropriate management of giant fibroepithelial
 breast lesions.

Background:
Organotropism describes the preferential spread of cancer cells to specific organs.
 Understanding this patterns in breast cancer may improve disease characterization and
 inform surveillance strategies. This study evaluated organ-specific metastatic
 involvement and radiological phenotypes in patients with breast cancer.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 A retrospective study was conducted using medical records from a tertiary referral center
 between July and December 2024. A total of 1,014 patients with metastases originating
 from five primary cancers were included. Site-specific metastatic frequencies, anatomical
 distributions, radiological phenotypes, and organ-specific metastases according to
 molecular subtype were evaluated. Categorical associations between breast cancer and
 radiological metastatic patterns were analyzed using the chi-square test with standardized
 residual analysis and compared with colorectal cancer.
Results:
Results
 In a cohort of 500 patients with metastatic breast cancer, bone was the most frequent site
 of distant metastasis, affecting 305 patients (61.0%), with the spine being the
 predominant skeletal location. Lung metastases were observed in 146 patients (29.2%),
 ranking as the second most common metastatic site. However, compared to colorectal
 cancer, breast cancer was associated with significantly lower odds of developing lung
 metastases (OR = 0.505, p = 0.005). Among patients with pulmonary metastases, breast
 cancer was significantly more likely than other primary malignancies to present with a
 pneumonic pattern (OR = 3.487, p < 0.001), which also tended to demonstrate unilateral
 distribution. Brain metastases were most located in the frontal and parietal lobes, and the
 HER2-enriched molecular subtype showed a higher prevalence of brain involvement than
 the other breast cancer subtypes.
Conclusion:
Breast cancer exhibits distinct organotropism characterized by predominant bone
 involvement and specific pulmonary and cerebral metastatic patterns. Differences in
 metastatic distribution highlight the biological heterogeneity of metastatic spread. These
 findings may support risk stratification, personalized imaging surveillance, and earlier
 detection of metastatic disease.

Background:

 alone, without axillary lymph node dissection (ALND), has non-inferior survival. However, it
 remains unclear how many SLNs should be harvested. We aimed to determine if the number
 of harvested SLNs affects oncological outcomes.

Methods
 From Jan 2020 to Jan 2026, T1-2 patients and 1-2 metastatic SLNs without ALND were
 prospectively enrolled and analyzed against patients who underwent ALND.
Results:
Results
 152 patients were enrolled, of which 63 and 89 underwent SLNB alone and ALND
 respectively. The 2 groups were comparable except that ALND group had more patients with
 mastectomy (p=0.0044), nodal radiation (p=0.0277) and macrometastasis (p=0.0001).
 Median number of harvested SLNs was 3(1-8) and 2(1-9) in the SLNB and ALND groups
 respectively. In the ALND group, residual median metastatic nodes of 1.5 (1-9) was seen in

 nodes. There was no recurrence after a median follow-up of 37 (3-75) months.

Background:
Background: Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women worldwide, with an
 estimated 2.3 million new cases and 666,000 deaths reported globally in 2022. Hand-Held Ultrasound
 (HHUS) is widely used for breast lesion detection but is limited by operator dependence and poor
 
 standardization. Automated Breast Ultrasound (ABUS) has emerged as a reproducible, operator-
 independent alternative enabling standardized whole-breast volumetric imaging. This systematic
 
 review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of ABUS compared with HHUS in detecting and
 characterizing breast lesions.
Materials & Methods:
Methods: A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Google Scholar, and Semantic Scholar.
 Studies comparing ABUS and HHUS diagnostic performance, reporting both sensitivity and
 specificity, were included regardless of comparison design (paired or parallel-group) or clinical setting;
 PPV, NPV, accuracy, and AUC were extracted as supplementary data where available. Risk of bias was
 assessed using QUADAS-2.
Results:
Results: Ten studies met the inclusion criteria. Reported sensitivity ranged from 60.0% to 95.7% for
 ABUS and 51.1% to 96.3% for HHUS, while specificity ranged from 70.0% to 97.8% for ABUS and
 49.4% to 96.7% for HHUS. Among the five studies reporting area under the curve (AUC), values
 ranged from 0.79 to 0.93 for ABUS and 0.72 to 0.93 for HHUS. Several studies reported significantly
 higher specificity and/or AUC for ABUS, while others reported comparable or higher sensitivity for
 HHUS, including one study in which HHUS outperformed ABUS across all reported parameters.
 Substantial heterogeneity was noted in comparison design, reference standards, and clinical context.
Conclusion:
Conclusion: ABUS demonstrates diagnostic performance broadly comparable to HHUS, with several
 studies favoring ABUS in specificity and/or AUC and others favoring HHUS in sensitivity. Given its
 operator-independent acquisition and reproducibility, ABUS may serve as a valuable complementary
 or alternative modality to HHUS, though heterogeneity in study design warrants cautious
 interpretation.

Background:
Dense breast reduces the sensitivity of full-field digital mammography to as low as 30-50%,
 because malignant lesions and normal fibroglandular parenchyma are both radiopaque and
 superimpose on a two-dimensional projection. Digital Breast Tomosynthesis (DBT) and breast
 MRI have been proposed to overcome this masking effect, yet their comparative accuracy
 remains contested. This review aims to comparatively evaluate the sensitivity and specificity
 of DBT versus breast MRI for breast cancer detection in women with dense breasts.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 A PRISMA 2020-based systematic review conducted across PubMed, Semantic Scholar, and
 Google Scholar. Eligible studies enrolled women with mammographically dense breasts (BI-
 RADS C-D) undergoing DBT and/or breast MRI, with at least one year of imaging follow-up
 as reference standard; reviews and studies without reported sensitivity and specificity were
 excluded. Of 2,134 screened records, 14 reports representing 13 studies met eligibility after
 title-abstract and full-text screening. Data on study design, population, index test parameters,
 reference standard, and the reported sensitivity and specificity values were extracted by a single
 reviewer into a standardized form. Methodological quality was appraised with QUADAS-2,
 and findings were synthesized narratively following the SWiM guideline.
Results:
Results
 Breast MRI showed higher sensitivity than DBT in every paired study, ranging 88.9-100.0%
 versus 39.1-96.4%. The widest gap occurred in the EA1141 prevalence round, where
 abbreviated MRI reached 95.7% against 39.1% for DBT in the same 1,444 women. Specificity
 favored DBT in screening populations (97.4-98.5% versus 86.7-93.3%), but this reversed in
 diagnostic cohorts (MRI 78.7-90.5%; DBT 52.8-81.0%). In the single density-stratified study,
 DBT sensitivity fell from 95.2% in BI-RADS A-C to 63.6% in BI-RADS D. Both modalities
 performed worse in the incidence round than the prevalence round.
Conclusion:
Breast MRI retains a consistent sensitivity advantage over DBT for breast cancer detection in
 dense breasts. While evidence is limited, DBT still offers superior overall screening specificity.

 and it frequently shows ultrasound features overlapping with benign lesions, which may delay
 diagnosis and worsen outcomes.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation: A 24-year-old woman presented with an enlarging left breast lump.
Ultrasound of the left breast showed a solid mass with an internal cystic component, up to 2.81 cm
in maximum diameter, classified BI-RADS 6 after a positive core-needle biopsy, alongside several
simple cysts (BI-RADS 2) and enlarged left axillary nodes up to 2.68 cm. Histology showed
invasive carcinoma, Nottingham grade 3, with lymphovascular invasion confirmed ER, PR and

Discussion: Central necrosis in high-grade TNBC can produce a complex cystic and solid

Background:

 multidisciplinary approach to mitigate surgical overtreatment. This study evaluates the
 clinical outcomes, malignancy upgrade rates, and long-term surveillance of ultrasound-
 guided vacuum-assisted biopsy (US-VAB) with therapeutic intent of complete lesion
 removal, assessing its role as a minimally invasive, tissue-sparing alternative to
 diagnostic open surgical excision.

Methods
 A retrospective cohort study evaluated consecutive core-needle biopsy-proven B3 papillary breast lesions without atypia, managed by therapeutic US-VAB (7- or 10-gauge needle) between April 2022 and March 2024.  and breast surgeons. Clinico-radiological, histopathological, and procedural data were analyzed. Technical success was defined as immediate, complete sonographic removal of the lesion. Results:
Results

 benign (B2) status. The overall malignant upgrade rate was 6.3% (4/64), identifying 3

 surgical excision.

Background:

 evidence comparing the diagnostic performance of standalone AI and radiologists remains

Methods

 mammographic examinations and 4,687 confirmed breast cancer cases were included. Eligible
 studies directly compared standalone AI and radiologists for mammographic breast cancer
 detection. Diagnostic accuracy data (TP, FP, FN, and TN) were extracted to estimate pooled
 sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), positive likelihood ratio (LR+), and negative
 likelihood ratio (LRâˆ’) using the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. Summary receiver
 operating characteristic (SROC) curves were generated, and heterogeneity was evaluated using
 Cochran's Q test and the I2 statistic.
Results:
Results
 Standalone AI demonstrated similar sensitivity to radiologists (60.8% vs 60.0%, p = 0.753).
 However, radiologists had higher specificity (97.8% vs 96.1%, p < 0.001), DOR (75.99 vs. 41.70,
 p = 0.001), and LR+ (28.40 vs 15.94, p < 0.001). There was no significant difference in LRâˆ’ (0.379
 vs 0.406, p = 0.151). Considerable heterogeneity was observed in most AI outcomes and in
 radiologist sensitivity.
Conclusion:
Standalone AI demonstrates similar sensitivity but lower overall diagnostic performance than
 radiologists. Currently, AI is better suited as a decision-support tool than as a replacement for
 radiologists in breast cancer screening. Further prospective studies are required to validate its
 performance in clinical practice.

Title:

Background:
To review the current global evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, and
 specificity of artificial intelligence (AI) deep learning algorithms in breast ultrasound.
 2. To visually demonstrate the characteristic sonographic features of benign and malignant
 breast lesions as interpreted by AI models versus human readers.
 3. To identify the clinical utility of AI in reducing inter-observer variability and minimizing
 unnecessary benign biopsies.

Content Organisation
This exhibit presents a systematic, PRISMA-guided review of 18 high-quality studies, encompassing over 15,000 breast ultrasound images through 2026. The content is structured into three main sections: (1) An overview of common AI architectures (CNN, ResNet, and Vision Transformers) used in breast imaging; (2) A side-by-side pictorial correlation of AI-segmented breast lesions (BI-RADS 3, 4, and 5) with their corresponding histopathological gold standards; and (3) A comparative analysis of diagnostic performance metrics, highlighting pooled sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC) variations.

1. Deep learning AI models demonstrate excellent pooled sensitivity (88.5%--94.2%) and robust specificity (82.1%--89.4%), yielding a high diagnostic accuracy with an overall AUC of 0.89--0.95.

Title:
Ultrasound Findings of Non-Mass Type Breast Tuberculosis: Beyond
 Typical Lesions
Authors: Rima Arini {1,3}, Lina Choridah {1}, Tri Wulan Handarini{2}
Affiliations:
1Gadjah Mada University Hospital, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
 2Soetomo general academic hospital, Surabaya, Indonesia.
 3General Hospital H. Adam Malik, Medan, Indonesia.
Keywords: Breast tuberculosis; ultrasound; lymph node; abscess; histopathological.
Background:
Breast tuberculosis can be either primary or secondary, but primary breast tuberculosis is
 extremely rare. If there is no other focus of infection elsewhere in the body, it is considered
 primary. The diagnosis of breast tuberculosis has three essential pillars: clinical examination,
 radiological evaluations, and histopathological sampling. Radiological evaluations are not only
 critical in diagnosis but are also important in the planning of the treatment and during the
 follow-up.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 26-year-old unmarried woman presented with a lump in her left breast and left axilla that had
 been present for six months. The lumps were enlarging and painful. The patient's mother had
 recently completed treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis the previous year. There were no
 respiratory complaints or history of pulmonary tuberculosis.
 Ultrasound findings revealed a hypoechoic lesion with ill-defined margins and focal distribution,
 accompanied by lactiferous duct dilatation and a sinus tract; no calcification or architectural
 distortion was observed. Multiple lymphadenopathies were also noted, some lacking a fatty
 hilum. The patient underwent excision, and histopathological analysis showed features
 suggestive of a specific chronic tuberculous inflammatory process with abscess formation.
Results:
Discussion
 Ultrasonography is often the first radiological examination method used in diagnosis. It is also
 the best method for evaluating axillary lymph nodes. Breast tuberculosis lesions can be
 classified into nodular, disseminated, sinus, or abscess type. In addition, alterations of axillary
 lymph nodes were also evaluated by US imaging.
Conclusion:
Breast tuberculosis is a difficult disease to diagnose, and clinical evaluation, radiological
 examination, histopathological and microbiological sampling are often necessary to confirm
 diagnosis. Radiological examinations are not only important in diagnosing the disease but are
 also important during the treatment and in the follow-up.

Title:
DIAGNOSTIC PERFORMANCE OF RADIOLOGIST AND REAL-TIME
 COMMERCIAL AI-ASSISTED TOOL BI-RADS IN CLASSIFYING BIOPSIED
 BREAST MASSES IN A SINGLE CENTRE: A PILOT STUDY
Authors: Nik Khairiyah Binti Raja MohammedÂ¹, Pang Fui Tin @ JaneÂ¹
Affiliations: Â¹Department of Radiology, Hospital Queen Elizabeth II, Sabah, Malaysia
Keywords: Diagnostic performance, ultrasound, AI-assisted tool, BI-RADS
Background:
Ultrasound interpretation of breast masses using BI-RADS is highly operator-dependent,
 causing notable interobserver variability. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools offer a
 promising solution to enhance diagnostic accuracy. This pilot study compares the diagnostic
 performance of a real-time commercial AI-assisted ultrasound system with radiologist-
 assigned BI-RADS classifications, using histopathological examination (HPE) as the
 reference standard.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 This prospective, single-centre study evaluated 18 biopsy-proven breast masses collected
 over a one-month period. Ultrasound images were interpreted by two breast imaging fellows
 and a commercial AI-tool. According to the BI-RADS lexicon, masses warranting biopsy are
 classified as BI-RADS 4 or higher; BI-RADS 3 masses typically do not require immediate
 biopsy. Thus, masses with an inherently low malignancy risk (2â€“10%) were assigned at least
 BI-RADS 4a to consider tissue biopsy. Diagnostic performance metrics were compared
 across two analytical frameworks: an original model (BI-RADS 4a treated as positive) and an
 adjusted model (BI-RADS 4a reclassified as negative).
Results:
Results
 Of the 18 masses, 6 (33.3%) were malignant and 12 (66.7%) were benign. All malignancies
 were correctly identified by both radiologists and AI-tool (assigned BI-RADS 4c or 5). For
 benign lesions, radiologists assigned BI-RADS 4a to all 12 cases, whereas the AI-tool
 classified 9 as BI-RADS 2, 2 as BI-RADS 4a, and 1 as BI-RADS 4c. In the original analysis,
 radiologists achieved 100% sensitivity and 0% specificity (AUC = 0.500), while the AI-tool
 demonstrated 100% sensitivity and 75.0% specificity (AUC = 0.875). In the adjusted
 framework, radiologists metrics shifted to 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity (AUC =
 1.000), while the AI-tool achieved 100% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity (AUC = 0.958).
Conclusion:
Both radiologists and AI-tool maintained excellent, uncompromised sensitivity. However, the
 commercial AI-tool demonstrated superior specificity by correctly downgrading most benign
 lesions, highlighting its clinical value in reducing unnecessary breast biopsies. These preliminary findings support integrating AI-assisted ultrasound systems as a supportive
 clinical adjunct.

Title:
A CASE SERIES OF GRANULOMATOUS MASTITIS OF THE BREAST: A
 RADIOLOGIC PERSPECTIVE ON A DIAGNOSTIC CHALLENGE
Authors: Nik Khairiyah Binti Raja MohammedÂ¹, Pang Fui Tin @ JaneÂ¹
Affiliations: Â¹Department of Radiology, Hospital Queen Elizabeth II, Sabah, Malaysia
Keywords:
Granulomatous mastitis, breast malignancy mimicker, histopathological examination, BI-
 RADS
Background:
Granulomatous mastitis is an uncommon inflammatory breast disease that poses a significant
 diagnostic challenge due to its ability to closely mimic breast malignancy. From January to
 December 2025, our centre diagnosed a total of 41 biopsy-proven cases of granulomatous,
 from which we retrospectively reviewed the clinical records, multimodality imaging findings,
 and histopathological outcomes of four selected female patients aged 33 to 63 years.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 Each case presented with a palpable breast lump but demonstrated a distinctly different
 sonographic pattern: Case 1 presented as a persistent heterogeneous hypoechoic abscess
 collection (BI-RADS 4a); Case 2 presented as a highly suspicious, irregular lobulated
 hypoechoic mass with focal asymmetry and distortion on mammography (BI-RADS 4c);
 Case 3 presented as an oval, circumscribed complex cyst containing soft tissue component
 (BI-RADS 4a); and Case 4 presented as a complicated cyst with mobile internal echogenicity
 (BI-RADS 4a).
Results:
Discussion
 Histopathological examination confirmed granulomatous inflammation for all patients.
 Interestingly, normal ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes were maintained across all cases.
 Differential diagnosis for granulomatous mastitis includes infectious (Mycobacterium
 tuberculosis, fungal, bacterial, or parasitic infections) or non-infectious causes (idiopathic,
 foreign-body reaction, trauma, autoimmune, or systemic disease). Because granulomatous
 mastitis exhibits highly diverse imaging features ranging from fluid collections to highly
 suspicious masses and lacks pathognomonic findings, prompt triple assessment and core
 needle biopsy remain the gold standard to establish an accurate diagnosis. Most often, no
 organism can be detected and it remains idiopathic.
Conclusion:
As granulomatous mastitis is frequently encountered and poses a diagnostic challenge in a
 tuberculosis-endemic region like Sabah, early recognition and meticulous histopathological
 evaluation are essential to distinguish idiopathic granulomatous mastitis from tuberculous
 mastitis, avoiding misdiagnosis and ensuring appropriate patient management.

Title:
CLINICAL AUDIT OF CASE-MIX, DIAGNOSTIC YIELD, AND PRACTICE
 PATTERNS: LESSONS AND SURPRISES FROM A NEWLY ESTABLISHED
 BREAST SERVICE IN JOHOR
Authors: Calvin Thomas John
Affiliations: Hospital Pasir Gudang, Masai, Johor, Malaysia
Keywords: breast biopsy, service audit, diagnostic yield, case-mix, HER2
Background:
Baseline case-mix and diagnostic performance data are valuable for guiding staffing,
 resource allocation and future service planning. However, such data are rarely available
 in a unit's first year. We conducted a clinical audit of core needle breast biopsies
 performed during the inaugural year of the breast diagnostic service at Hospital Pasir
 Gudang (HPG), Johor.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
This retrospective clinical audit included all core needle breast biopsies performed in the first 12 months since inception of the breast diagnostic service at HPG— a complete, anonymized series of 91 patients. Each histopathology report was classified by diagnostic category; biopsy method, i.e. either clinically (“blind”/palpation-guided) or radiologically (ultrasound/mammogram-guided); and tissue adequacy per the histopathological report. Receptor profile (ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67) was recorded for invasive carcinomas, tested at a single reference laboratory. Adequacy across methods was compared using Fisher's exact test.
Results:
Results
Of 91 biopsies, 28 (30.8%) yielded malignancies (25 invasive carcinoma, 3 pure ductal carcinoma in situ), 26 (28.6%) were fibroepithelial lesions, 6 (6.6%) were inflammatory (mastitis, abscess, or granulomatous), and 31 (34.1%) were other benign findings. Among invasive carcinomas, 13 of 24 tested (54%) were HER2-positive, higher than the 20-30% in regional Malaysian and Asian cohorts. Most biopsies (61, 67%) were performed blind; adequacy was 80.3% for blind versus 85.7% for ultrasound-guided biopsy, a non-significant difference (Fisher's exact p=0.77). Twelve blind biopsies required repeat sampling, including one failed blind biopsy later confirmed as papillary neoplasm on repeat ultrasound-guided biopsy.
Conclusion:
This first-year clinical audit establishes baseline case-mix and diagnostic yield for a
 breast diagnostic service. A substantial malignancy rate and a notably high, possibly
 referral-biased, HER2-positivity rate highlight the value of early-service data for future
 oncology and breast surgery service planning. Blind biopsy adequacy was numerically,
 though not significantly, lower than ultrasound-guided biopsy, and its repeat-biopsy
 burden is a target for practice improvement.

Title:
FROM MRI TO BIOPSY: CONTRAST-ENHANCED DIGITAL MAMMOGRAPHY AS A
 DIAGNOSTIC BRIDGE FOR OCCULT CONTRALATERAL BREAST LESIONS

Keywords:

 Guided Biopsy; Contralateral Breast Cancer
Background:
Learning Objectives:
 Â· To demonstrate the role of contrast-enhanced digital mammography (CEDM) as an effective and
 accessible alternative to MRI-guided biopsy for MRI-detected non-mass enhancement (NME)
 without ultrasound correlation.
 Â· To illustrate the imaging-pathology correlation of CEDM-detected occult synchronous
 contralateral breast lesions.
 Â· To discuss a practical diagnostic approach when MRI-guided breast intervention is unavailable.
Materials & Methods:
Content Organisation:
 A 59-year-old woman with no significant breast cancer risk factors presented with a 3-month history of a
 self-detected right breast lump, although no palpable abnormality was found on clinical examination.
 Initial mammography and ultrasound demonstrated suspicious grouped calcifications, with stereotactic
 biopsy confirming right breast carcinoma in situ (CIS). Preoperative breast MRI demonstrated bilateral
 NME, including an additional focal NME in the left upper outer quadrant (LUOQ) without a
 mammographic or sonographic correlate. As MRI-guided biopsy was unavailable locally, CEDM was
 performed and demonstrated corresponding moderate intensity enhancement of the LUOQ lesion.
 CEDM-guided biopsy with marker clip placement confirmed synchronous invasive carcinoma. This case
 reviews the multimodality imaging findings, technical aspects of CEDM-guided biopsy, imaging-
 pathology correlation, and the impact on subsequent patient management.
Results:
Key Teaching Points:
 -CEDM is a valuable problem-solving tool for MRI-detected lesions without an ultrasound correlate.
 -When a corresponding enhancing lesion is identified, CEDM-guided biopsy provides a practical and cost-
 effective alternative to MRI-guided biopsy. -Contrast-enhanced breast imaging may reveal otherwise
 occult synchronous contralateral malignancy, significantly influencing surgical planning and treatment.
Conclusion:
CEDM is a valuable diagnostic and interventional alternative for MRI-detected, mammographically and
 sonographically occult breast lesions when MRI-guided biopsy is unavailable, enabling accurate lesion
 localisation, tissue diagnosis, and timely management.

Title:
MULTIMODALITY IMAGING OF SYNCHRONOUS BILATERAL AND
 IPSILATERAL BREAST CANCERS WITH DISTINCT HISTOLOGICAL
 
 SUBTYPES: A CASE SERIES
Authors: Dalila Badrul HishamÂ¹, Nor Asnani Mohd RamliÂ¹
Affiliations: Â¹Hospital Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Keywords:
Synchronous breast cancer; mucinous carcinoma; invasive carcinoma NST;
 contrast-enhanced mammography; multimodality imaging
Background:
Synchronous breast cancer is an uncommon presentation that may occur as bilateral or
 ipsilateral primary malignancies diagnosed within six months. Distinct histological
 subtypes within synchronous tumours present diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.
 Multimodality imaging is essential for lesion detection, radiologicâ€“pathologic correlation,
 staging and treatment planning.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 Two patients with synchronous breast cancer are presented. A 59-year-old asymptomatic
 postmenopausal woman had bilateral screen-detected lesions. Mammography,
 ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) with image-guided
 biopsies demonstrated right invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST) and left
 mucinous carcinoma. A 46-year-old woman presented with a palpable right breast lump,
 and imaging identified two ipsilateral lesions proven as invasive carcinoma NST and
 mucinous carcinoma. No distant metastases were detected in either patient. Bilateral
 mastectomy was performed in the first patient, while the second underwent nipple-
 sparing mastectomy with axillary clearance and immediate reconstruction. Final
 histopathology confirmed node-negative disease with clear margins. Both patients
 received planned adjuvant endocrine therapy.
Results:
Discussion
 These cases highlight the heterogeneous imaging appearances of synchronous breast
 cancers and emphasise that lesions with benign imaging features, particularly mucinous
 carcinoma, may coexist with more aggressive malignancies. Independent assessment and
 biopsy of each suspicious lesion are essential. Mammography, ultrasonography and CEM provide complementary information for accurate diagnosis, staging and surgical
 planning.
Conclusion:
Recognition of synchronous breast cancers with distinct histological subtypes is essential
 for optimal multidisciplinary management. Comprehensive multimodality imaging and
 radiologicâ€“pathologic correlation facilitate accurate diagnosis and individualised
 treatment.

Title:
METACHRONOUS OVARIAN MALIGNANCY IN TRIPLE-NEGATIVE BREAST
 CANCER SUSPECTED OF HEREDITARY BREAST OVARIAN CANCER SYNDROME
Authors: Fitri Andriani 1,4 , Lina Choridah 2 , Mirna Muis 3
Affiliations:

 2 Faculty of Medicine Public Health and Nursing Gajah Mada University, Indonesia
 3 Faculty of Medicine, Hasanuddin University, Indonesia
 4 Awalbros Hospital Pekanbaru, Indonesia
Keywords:
Triple-negative breast cancer; bilateral ovarian mass; Hereditary Breast and Ovarian
 Cancer (HBOC) syndrome; Genetic test BRCA1/BRCA2
Background:
Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype strongly associated
 with hereditary cancer predisposition, particularly Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer
 (HBOC) syndrome caused by germline BRCA1/BRCA2 pathogenic variants. Young-onset
 TNBC is a recognized indication for hereditary cancer risk assessment, and subsequent ovarian
 malignancy further increases suspicion of HBOC.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
A 32-year-old woman with an unavailable family history of malignancy presented with a palpable mass in the upper medial quadrant of the right breast. Histopathological examination confirmed TNBC (invasive carcinoma of no special type, grade II) with lymphovascular space invasion. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated estrogen receptor-negative, progesterone receptor-negative, HER2-negative status, and a Ki-67 proliferation index >80%. Following modified radical mastectomy, she received adjuvant chemotherapy and locoregional radiotherapy. One month later, contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated multiple osteolytic skeletal metastases, and palliative radiotherapy with bone-targeted therapy was initiated. 
Approximately one year later, markedly elevated CEA and CA15-3 levels, pleural effusion, and a pelvic mass prompted contrast-enhanced pelvic MRI, which demonstrated bilateral predominantly solid ovarian masses with heterogeneous enhancement and multiple osseous metastases. Based on the patient’s history of metastatic TNBC and the imaging findings, the lesions were initially interpreted as bilateral ovarian metastases. However, histopathological examination following total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and omentectomy revealed a mixed adult-type granulosa cell tumor with a moderately differentiated mucinous carcinoma component involving both ovaries, confirming a metachronous second primary ovarian malignancy..
Results:
Discussion
 Young-onset TNBC followed by primary ovarian malignancy should prompt consideration of
 HBOC, even when family history is unavailable. Although the ovarian histology was atypical for
 BRCA-associated ovarian cancer and genetic confirmation was unavailable, this presentation
 fulfills established criteria for genetic counseling and germline BRCA1/BRCA2 or hereditary
 cancer multigene panel testing.
Conclusion:
This case highlights that atypical ovarian histology should not preclude hereditary cancer risk
 assessment in patients with young onset TNBC. Early recognition of hereditary cancer risk is
 essential to guide genetic counselling and germline testing, personalized management, optimize
 surveillance, and facilitate cancer risk assessment for at-risk family members.

Title: MULTIPARAMETRIC ULTRASOUND IN NEOADJUVANT-TREATED MALE BREAST CANCER
Authors: Pramesti Indri MirantiÂ¹Â², Lina ChoridahÂ³, Mirna Muis 4
Affiliations:
Fellowship Women Imaging, RSA UGM, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
 Â² Department of Radiology, Dr. Hasan Sadikin General Hospital, Bandung, Indonesia
 Â³ Department of Radiology, Faculty of Medicine, Public Health and Nursing, Universitas
 Gadjah Madaâ€“Dr. Sardjito General Hospital, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
 4 Department of Radiology, Hasanuddin University, Makassar, Indonesia
Keywords:
Male breast cancer; Neoadjuvant chemotherapy; Multiparametric ultrasound;
 Strain elastography
Background: Male breast cancer accounts for less than 1% of all breast malignancies, with limited evidence regarding imaging assessment after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). Accurate response evaluation is essential for treatment planning. Multiparametric breast ultrasound combining B-mode imaging, Doppler, and strain elastography may provide information beyond tumor size. We present a case highlighting its potential role in monitoring NAC response in male breast cancer.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
A 53-year-old man presented with a progressively enlarging painless left breast mass, nipple retraction, and intermittent bloody nipple discharge. Core needle biopsy confirmed grade III invasive carcinoma of no special type with lymphovascular invasion and associated high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ. Baseline ultrasound demonstrated a 23 × 18 cm irregular heterogeneous infiltrative mass involving all quadrants of the left breast, with intralesional calcifications, posterior acoustic shadowing, increased internal and peripheral vascularity, a strain ratio of 4.5, and left axillary level II lymphadenopathy. Following NAC, ultrasound showed modest tumor reduction (20 × 16 cm), resolution of axillary lymphadenopathy, and an increased strain ratio to 6.0. The patient subsequently underwent modified radical mastectomy
Results:
Discussion
 Breast MRI is the reference standard for NAC response assessment but may not always be available. Previous studies, predominantly in female breast cancer, have associated treatment response with reduced tumor stiffness on elastography. In contrast, this case demonstrated increased stiffness despite modest tumor shrinkage and nodal resolution, revealing discordant elastographic, dimensional, and nodal responses. This underscores the need to interpret elastography within a multiparametric framework rather than as an isolated response marker. Lack of postoperative pathological response data limits imaging–pathology correlation.
Conclusion: Multiparametric breast ultrasound provides complementary information beyond tumor size in monitoring NAC response. Discordance between dimensional, nodal, and elastographic findings underscores the importance of multiparametric interpretation and pathological correlation for accurate treatment response assessment.

Title: THE TALE OF TWO BREASTS: SYNCHRONOUS RIGHT BREAST LYMPHOMA AND LEFT BREAST INVASIVE CARCINOMA
Authors: Dr. Nur Haneefa binti Ahmad1, Dr. Wan Mezlina binti Wan Zakaria1, Dr. Laily Syakimah binti Saidi1, Dr. Zahurin binti Ismail1
Affiliations: Hospital Putrajaya, Putrajaya, Malaysia
Keywords: Synchronous breast malignancies, breast lymphoma, invasive breast carcinoma, multidisciplinary breast team management.
Background: Synchronous bilateral breast malignancies with different histological subtypes are exceedingly rare. The coexistence of breast lymphoma and invasive breast carcinoma presents a unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenge. We present a rare case of synchronous right breast diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and left breast invasive breast carcinoma, highlighting the importance of multimodality imaging and histopathological confirmation of each lesion.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 55-year-old woman presented with bilateral breast swelling. The left breast swelling was initially presumed to be an abscess, subsequently rupturing with persistent purulent discharge and incomplete healing.
 Mammography demonstrated bilateral suspicious breast masses with bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy (BI-RADS 5). Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed bilateral breast masses with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pulmonary nodules, and osseous lesions suspicious for metastatic disease.
 Histopathology revealed two distinct malignancies. The left breast lesion was invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (Grade 2), ER-positive, PR-positive, and HER2-negative. The right breast lesion was high-grade B-cell lymphoma consistent with DLBCL, positive for CD20 and BCL2 with a Ki-67 proliferative index of 95%. Biopsy of the right axillary lymph node demonstrated metastatic carcinoma, likely originating from the contralateral breast carcinoma. The patient was subsequently referred to the Haematology team for further management of the breast lymphoma.
Results:
Discussion
 Breast lymphoma accounts for less than 1% of all breast malignancies, and its synchronous occurrence with invasive breast carcinoma is exceptionally uncommon. This case underscores the importance of independently evaluating bilateral breast lesions, as they may represent distinct pathological entities rather than multifocal or metastatic disease. Accurate radiological characterisation and histopathological confirmation are essential, particularly when treatment approaches differ significantly.
 Beyond establishing the diagnosis, this case highlights the pivotal role of breast imaging in multidisciplinary decision-making. The identification of two distinct malignancies altered the patient's management pathway, necessitating coordinated care involving breast radiologists, breast surgeons, pathologists, medical oncologists, and haematologists. While invasive breast carcinoma is commonly managed with a combination of surgery and receptor-directed systemic therapy, breast lymphoma is primarily treated with systemic chemo-immunotherapy. Recognising synchronous malignancies at the diagnostic stage facilitates appropriate referral pathways and enables timely initiation of disease-specific treatment. This case exemplifies the indispensable role of the multidisciplinary breast team in delivering personalised and coordinated patient care.
Conclusion: Synchronous breast lymphoma and invasive breast carcinoma, although rare, should be considered in patients presenting with bilateral suspicious breast lesions. Multimodality imaging and histopathological confirmation of each lesion, is crucial in avoiding diagnostic pitfalls and ensuring appropriate multidisciplinary management.

Title:

 CHALLENGE

Keywords:

 ultrasonography; benign breast disease; hepatic haemangioma
Background:
Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM) is an uncommon benign chronic inflammatory
 breast condition affecting women of reproductive age. Its clinical and radiological
 features overlap with breast malignancy. We report IGM mimicking locally advanced
 malignancy, with suspicious axillary and incidental hepatic findings evaluated by
 multimodality imaging.
Materials & Methods:
Case
 A 42-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of right breast pain and
 swelling. Breast ultrasonography demonstrated irregular heterogeneous hypoechoic area
 in the right upper outer quadrant and an enlarged ipsilateral axillary lymph node with
 cortical thickening. Contrast-enhanced mammography showed non-mass enhancement
 with washout and an enhancing axillary node, raising suspicion of malignancy.
 Abdominal ultrasonography identified hyperechoic and hypoechoic hepatic lesions.
 Staging computed tomography demonstrated enhancing liver lesions. Magnetic resonance
 imaging confirmed benign haemangiomas, excluding metastases. Ultrasound-guided core
 biopsy showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation without malignancy or
 specific infection, confirming granulomatous mastitis. Oral corticosteroids resulted in
 improvement with resolution of pain and inflammatory changes.
Results:
Discussion
 IGM can resemble locally advanced breast cancer on ultrasonography and contrast-
 enhanced mammography. Axillary lymphadenopathy and indeterminate hepatic lesions
 may heighten concern for nodal and distant metastases. Further imaging confirmed the
 liver lesions as benign haemangiomas, avoiding their misclassification as metastatic
 disease. Nevertheless, imaging features are non-specific and cannot reliably differentiate
 IGM from malignancy.
Conclusion:
IGM should be considered in women with inflammatory breast symptoms and suspicious
 imaging findings. Multimodality imaging helps assess disease extent and characterise
 incidental lesions, but histopathology remains essential to exclude malignancy and
 specific infection and ensure appropriate treatment.

Title:

 TOMOSYNTHESIS IN A TERTIARY HOSPITAL
Authors:

Background:
Screening mammography reduces mortality, but its sensitivity drops in dense breast
 tissue. Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) combined with full field digital
 mammography (FFDM) improves lesion visualization and cancer detection, especially in
 dense breasts. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of DBT at a Malaysian
 tertiary referral center.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 This retrospective study examined 1,064 women undergoing combined DBT and FFDM
 between January and December 2019. Participants were divided into opportunistic
 screening, targeted screening and diagnostic groups. Patients with prior
 histopathologically confirmed malignancy, implants, reconstructed breasts or previous
 surgery were excluded. Images were interpreted using the standard ACR-BIRADS
 lexicon, with final categories determined after adjunct ultrasound evaluation.
 Histopathological results from biopsy were used as the reference standard to evaluate
 sensitivity, specificity and predictive values.
Results:
Results
 Among 392 lesions detected on tomosynthesis, 159 were confirmed malignant, yielding a
 positive predictive value (PPV) of 40.4%. Three additional ultrasound detected lesions
 brought the total to 162 malignancies, including 108 in the diagnostic group, 41 in
 opportunistic screening and 13 in targeted screening. PPV of screen-detected lesions
 presented as masses for BIRADS 4a, 4b, and 4c category were 17.8%, 35.1%, and 60.2%,
 respectively. The sensitivity, specificity, PPV and negative predictive value (NPV) of
 mass lesions was 92.5%, 84%, 87.5%, and 90.2%, respectively. The cancer detection rate
 of 3 different cohorts was the opportunistic screening group (54.5 cancers per 1,000
 screenings), the targeted screening group (112.1 cancers per 1,000 screenings), and the
  diagnostic group (484.3 cancers per 1,000 examinations). PPV3 of calcification is 59.8%,
 and asymmetry is 50%.
Conclusion:
DBT is effective for screening and diagnostic breast imaging, improving early cancer
 detection in opportunistic screening settings in Malaysia. Multicentre prospective studies
 are recommended.

Title:

 COMPARING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE WITH RADIOLOGISTS
Authors: Siti Naqiiah Saari, Suraya A Aziz
Affiliations:

 Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Keywords:
Artificial intelligence; Mammography; Breast cancer; Diagnostic
 performance; Radiologists
Background:
Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women worldwide and early
 detection through mammographic screening is essential for reducing mortality. Artificial
 intelligence (AI) has emerged as a potential adjunct to radiologists in mammography
 interpretation. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of an AI system
 in breast cancer detection on two-dimensional (2D) mammography and compare its
 performance with radiologists
Materials & Methods:
Methods
A cross-sectional study was conducted using 212 anonymised 2D mammography cases from a tertiary healthcare centre. Histopathological examination served as the gold standard. Mammograms were analysed using an AI software platform and independently reviewed by two radiologists. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results:
Results

Conclusion:

Background:

 an estimated incidence of 2.4 per 100,000 women. Because its clinical and imaging
 features frequently mimic breast carcinoma, radiologists play a crucial role in recognizing
 suspicious imaging patterns and directing appropriate image-guided biopsy.
