Case Presentation
 A 36-year-old non-lactating woman presented with a painful left breast lump that
 progressed to recurrent breast abscesses over one year despite repeated antibiotic therapy
 and ultrasound-guided aspirations. Initial ultrasound demonstrated an irregular
 hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic shadowing, raising suspicion for malignancy.
 Follow-up ultrasound revealed progression into an irregular hypoechoic lesion with
 characteristic finger-like tubular extensions tracking between breast lobules, associated
 with multiloculated abscess collections. Given the persistent suspicious imaging findings,
 ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy targeted the viable solid component of the lesion.

 inflammatory infiltrates without atypia or acid-fast bacilli. The patient was managed
 conservatively with corticosteroid therapy, with serial ultrasound demonstrating gradual
 resolution of the inflammatory collections.
Results:
Discussion
 CGM has no pathognomonic imaging appearance and frequently overlaps with breast
 malignancy. However, irregular hypoechoic lesions with interconnected tubular or finger-
 like extensions and associated abscesses should raise suspicion for CGM, particularly in
 young non-lactating women with recurrent mastitis unresponsive to antibiotics.
 Ultrasound is invaluable for lesion characterization and guiding core biopsy of viable
 inflammatory tissue while avoiding liquefied necrotic areas, enabling accurate diagnosis
 and exclusion of malignancy. As recurrence is common and rare cases of coexisting
 breast carcinoma have been reported, long-term clinical and imaging surveillance is
 recommended until complete resolution.
Conclusion:
Recognizing the evolving ultrasound pattern of CGM can shift the pathway from repeated
 abscess treatment to tissue diagnosis, guide conservative management, and monitor
 resolutionâ€”while avoiding unnecessary surgery for a benign condition mimicking breast
 carcinoma.

 approach.

 of gel fillers and their related complications is useful for making an accurate diagnosis.

 assessment to establish the correct diagnosis.

Case Presentation

 salpingo-oophorectomy (TAHBSO) for uterine fibroids presented with a painful right
 retro-areolar lump of three weeks' duration. She denied fever or preceding trauma. She
 was referred to the Breast Imaging Unit as an urgent case via Pink Ribbon Clinic. The
 primary surgeon was worried that this may be a suspicious lesion for malignancy. This
 prompted triple assessment using CEM as the primary modality. Contrast-enhanced
 mammography (CEM) demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing right retro-areolar
 lesion. Targeted ultrasound showed a corresponding, indeterminate solid retro-areolar
 lesion with peripheral vascularity.

 reduction in lesion size with partial liquefaction, and the patient reported clinical

Discussion

 excluding malignancy and establishing diagnosis. The presence of budding yeast on PAS

 importance of clinicopathological correlation. Close collaboration between radiologists,

 management and ensures that occult breast malignancy is not overlooked.

Awareness of this rare radiological mimic and the integration of clinical, imaging,

 diagnosis, guiding appropriate management, avoiding unnecessary treatment, and
 ensuring timely exclusion of underlying breast cancer.

Background:

 undefined across practices. The trial was designed to compare the rate of complete clinical
 resolution (CCR) of IGM at ten weeks between high-dose and low-dose regimen, while
 evaluating which regimen provides a more favourable safety profile.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 A multicentre, single-blinded randomised controlled trial was conducted across five centres in
 Malaysia, recruiting patients with histologically confirmed IGM over two years. Baseline data on
 demographic characteristics, clinical signs and symptoms, inflammatory markers and ultrasound
 characteristics were collected. The primary objective was CCR at 10 weeks. Secondary
 objectives include radiological resolution and safety profile comparison.
Results:
Results
 36 patients were randomised 1:1 to high-dose (1.0 mg/kg/day, n=18) or low-dose prednisolone
 (0.5 mg/kg/day, n=18), with standardised fortnightly dose reduction over 10 weeks with
 confirmed baseline comparability between arms. CCR was achieved in 17 (94.4%) patients in
 low-dose versus 13 (72.2%) in high-dose arm (p=0.072). Treatment failure occurred exclusively

 One adverse event was recorded in high-dose and none in low-dose arm (p=1.000).
Conclusion:

 high-dose arm. From a clinical standpoint, these findings do not support routine dose initiation at
 1.0 mg/kg/day. Low-dose prednisolone is identified as the preferred first-line regimen in IGM,

Background:

 with highly discordant imaging characteristics. We report an unusual mammographic

 densities in a patient with a history of a previously excised fibroadenoma.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
 A 61-year-old woman presented with a right breast lump that had been stable since 2014

 included a right breast lumpectomy in 2009 for a histologically proven fibroadenoma.
 Mammography revealed two large, well-circumscribed right breast masses with
 discordant densities, which collectively caused gross distortion of the breast contour and
 flattening of the nipple. The posterior mass was predominantly of soft-tissue density. In
 contrast, the adjacent retroareolar mass was fat-dominant, with extensive, coarse linear

 differing echogenicities and internal vascularity.

 with phyllodes tumour and giant postsurgical fat necrosis as the differentials. Ultrasound-

 correlation, targeting both the soft-tissue mass and the fat-containing mass with
 calcification. Histopathological results are currently pending.

Discussion
 The coexistence of two adjacent giant breast masses with contrasting imaging
 characteristics; specifically, a soft-tissue-density mass abutting a fat-dominant mass with
 prominent branching calcifications presents an unusual diagnostic challenge. Recognition
 of these atypical imaging findings and targeted sampling of each distinct radiological
 component is important to ensure precise pathological correlation and guide
 multidisciplinary management.
Conclusion:
This case highlights a rare presentation of adjacent giant breast masses with discordant
 imaging characteristics. It emphasizes the critical role of recognizing atypical imaging
 features and obtaining representative, multi-site tissue samples to avoid diagnostic pitfalls

 breast cancer remains the leading cancer among women. It then outlines the technical basis of
 ultrafast MRI, contrasting its high temporal resolution (images every 2â€“10 seconds) with
 conventional DCE-MRI (every 60â€“120 seconds). Findings from our institutionâ€™s 2025 screening
 experience, comprising 109 breast MRI examinations, are presented, comparing sensitivity and
 specificity between ultrafast and conventional MRI, followed by illustrative cases spanning
 invasive carcinoma, dense breasts, filler injections and nipple discharge, correlating imaging  findings with histopathology.

 examples further illustrate its value in dense breasts post-filler and breast cancer imaging,

Ultrafast breast MRI offers a fast, accurate and scalable adjunct to conventional breast MRI,

 the primary malignancy. Failure to recognize a metastatic origin may result in incorrect
 staging, unnecessary breast-directed surgery, and inappropriate treatment.

Case Presentation
 A 43-year-old female with chief complaint of abdominal distension and suspected ovarian
 malignancy from prior hospital was referred to our hospital for surgery and chemotherapy.

 ovary, suggestive of malignancy. Patients underwent surgery followed by chemotherapy.

Discussion

 with known extramammary malignancy, breast metastases should be considered in
 differential diagnosis rather than favoring only on morphological assessment.

Background:

Methods:

Results:

 during BCAM and 395 (41.9%) during non-BCAM periods. BI-RADS 2 was the most

Discussion
 Primary breast MALT lymphoma is an uncommon but important differential
 diagnosis for suspicious breast lesions. Although imaging findings overlap
 with breast cancer, histopathological confirmation is essential. Cross-sectional
 imaging plays a pivotal role in staging, detecting occult extra-mammary
 disease and guiding lymphoma-directed management while avoiding
 unnecessary breast surgery.
Conclusion:
Primary breast MALT lymphoma should be considered in the differential
 diagnosis of suspicious screen-detected breast lesions. Multimodality
 imaging, histopathological confirmation and multidisciplinary collaboration are
 essential for accurate diagnosis, comprehensive staging and appropriate
 patient management.

Title: Beyond the Index Lesion: The Added Value of Breast MRI in Invasive Lobular Carcinoma — A Two-Case Series
Authors:
Dr. Nur Haneefa binti Ahmad 1 , Dr. Wan Mezlina binti Wan Zakaria 1 , Dr. Laily Syakimah
 binti Saidi 1 , Dr. Zahurin binti Ismail 1
Affiliations: 1 Hospital Putrajaya, Wilayah Persekutuan Putrajaya, Malaysia
Keywords: Invasive lobular carcinoma, Lobular carcinoma in situ, breast MRI, local staging
Background: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is the second most common invasive breast malignancy, accounting for 5–15% of cases. Its infiltrative growth pattern may result in underestimation of disease extent on conventional imaging. Contrast-enhanced breast MRI has high sensitivity for ILC and plays an important role in local staging. We present two cases illustrating its added value in detecting additional ipsilateral and contralateral disease.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
Case 1: A 55-year-old woman presented with a right breast lump. Mammography and ultrasound demonstrated a highly suspicious right breast mass with satellite lesions and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of the right breast mass confirmed ILC, while the left axillary lymph node demonstrated metastatic carcinoma. Breast MRI demonstrated multifocal right breast disease and an additional suspicious left breast lesion at 4 o’clock. Biopsy of the left breast lesion confirmed ILC, establishing bilateral breast malignancy. The patient was started on chemotherapy with palliative intent.
Case 2: A 44-year-old woman presented with a right breast lump. Mammography and ultrasound demonstrated a suspicious right breast lesion at 11 o’clock, with biopsy confirming ILC. MRI demonstrated the known malignant mass and an additional suspicious right breast lesion at 9 o’clock. Biopsy of the additional lesion confirmed ILC with lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS). The patient underwent right wide local excision with bilateral reduction mammoplasty. Postoperative histopathology demonstrated multiple foci of ILC and LCIS in the right breast and left LCIS, confirming more extensive multifocal disease.
Results:
Discussion
 These cases demonstrate the added value of breast MRI in defining disease extent in ILC,
 which may be underestimated on conventional imaging due to its infiltrative growth pattern.
 Breast MRI identified contralateral malignancy in the first case and additional ipsilateral
 disease in the second, providing clinically relevant information for management planning.
Conclusion:
Breast MRI is essential in local staging of ILC, enabling detection of additional ipsilateral
 and contralateral disease and facilitating appropriate biopsy, staging, and individualized
 surgical planning.

 ELASTOGRAPHY GUIDED BIOPSY IN BIRADS 4 AND 5 BREAST LESIONS.

Keywords: SWE, Breast Biopsy, BI-RADS, Neoplasm.
Background:
Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy is a standard method for sampling breast lesions.
 Despite its high diagnostic accuracy, sampling error may occur due to intratumoral
 heterogeneity. Shear wave elastography (SWE) may identify areas of differing tissue
 stiffness and potentially guide targeted sampling. This study evaluates SWE
 characteristics between high- and low-stiffness areas within the same breast lesion and
 their association with histopathological diagnosis.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 This cross-sectional diagnostic study included patients with BI-RADS 4 and 5 breast
 lesions referred for mammography and ultrasound assessment. Ultrasound-guided core
 needle biopsy and SWE assessment were performed on the same day. Quantitative SWE
 parameters, including maximum SWE, mean SWE, and maximum-to-minimum SWE
 ratio, were obtained from visually hard and soft regions within each lesion. Qualitative
 SWE color scores were also recorded and correlated with histopathological findings. The
 Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for paired comparisons between hard and soft
 regions, while the Mannâ€“Whitney U test compared SWE parameters between benign and
 malignant lesions. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results:
Results
 Among 37 lesions with complete quantitative SWE data, maximum and mean SWE
 values were significantly higher in hard than soft regions (both p<0.001), with higher
 values observed in all 37 lesions. The hard-region SWE ratio was also significantly
 higher than the soft-region ratio (p<0.001). Among benign (n=26) and malignant (n=11)
 lesions, malignant lesions demonstrated higher maximum and mean hard-region SWE
 values, although these differences did not reach statistical significance (p=0.065 and
 p=0.058, respectively). No significant differences were observed in soft-region SWE
 parameters. Qualitative SWE demonstrated a distinct shift toward higher color scores in
 malignant lesions; 63.6% had a score of 5 and 27.3% a score of 4, whereas all benign
 lesions had scores of 2 or 3.
Conclusion:
SWE demonstrated significant differences between hard and soft regions within breast
 lesions, supporting its potential role in identifying intratumoral stiffness heterogeneity.
 Qualitative SWE color scoring showed a distinct association with malignancy and may
 provide additional information for targeted assessment and biopsy of heterogeneous
 breast lesions.

Title: MULTIPARAMETRIC ULTRASOUND IN NEOADJUVANT-TREATED MALE BREAST CANCER

Keywords:
Male breast cancer; Neoadjuvant chemotherapy; Multiparametric ultrasound;
 Doppler ultrasound; Strain elastography
Background:
Male breast cancer accounts for less than 1% of all breast malignancies, with limited
 evidence regarding imaging assessment after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). Accurate
 response evaluation is essential for treatment planning. Multiparametric breast ultrasound
 combining B-mode imaging, Doppler, and strain elastography may provide information
 beyond tumor size. We present a case highlighting its potential role in monitoring NAC
 response in male breast cancer.
Materials & Methods:
Case Presentation
A 53-year-old man presented with a progressively enlarging painless left breast mass, nipple retraction, and intermittent bloody nipple discharge. Core needle biopsy confirmed grade III invasive carcinoma of no special type with lymphovascular invasion and associated high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ. Baseline ultrasound demonstrated a 23 × 18 cm irregular heterogeneous infiltrative mass involving all quadrants of the left breast, with intralesional calcifications, posterior acoustic shadowing, increased internal and peripheral vascularity, a strain ratio of 4.5, and left axillary level II lymphadenopathy. Following NAC, ultrasound showed modest tumor reduction (20 × 16 cm), resolution of axillary lymphadenopathy, and an increased strain ratio to 6.0. The patient subsequently underwent modified radical mastectomy.
Results:
Discussion
Breast MRI is the reference standard for NAC response assessment but may not always be available. Previous studies, predominantly in female breast cancer, have associated treatment response with reduced tumor stiffness on elastography. In contrast, this case demonstrated increased stiffness despite modest tumor shrinkage and nodal resolution, revealing discordant elastographic, dimensional, and nodal responses. This underscores the need to interpret elastography within a multiparametric framework rather than as an isolated response marker. Lack of postoperative pathological response data limits imaging–pathology correlation.
Conclusion: Multiparametric breast ultrasound provides complementary information beyond tumor size in monitoring NAC response. Discordance between dimensional, nodal, and elastographic findings underscores the importance of multiparametric interpretation and pathological correlation for accurate treatment response assessment.

Keywords: ultrasonography, breast neoplasms, strain ratio, elastography
Background:
Strain elastography (SE), which assesses tissue stiffness, has emerged as a promising adjunct
 to conventional B-mode ultrasound (USG) in diagnostic accuracy of breast lesions. Our study
 aimed to determine the diagnostic performance of two parameters of SE, namely elasticity
 index to B-mode ratio (E I /B ratio) and strain ratio (SR) in differentiating benign and
 malignant solid Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) 4 lesions with HPE
 correlation.
Materials & Methods:
Methods
 This cross sectional, single centre study included a total of 317 samples. The BI-RADS
 categories were determined from conventional B-mode USG features. Then E I /B ratio and SR
 were measured and biopsies taken as part of management of BI-RADS 4 lesions. The
 receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were constructed to determine the cut-off
 values, as well as to compare the diagnostic performances of each parameters.
Results:
Results
 264 benign and 53 malignant lesions were diagnosed. The optimal cut- off value for E I /B
 ratio and SR was 1.1 and 2.39, respectively, which shows statistically significant difference
 between benign and malignant lesions (p < 0.001 and p = 0.0337, respectively). When
 combining E I /B ratio and SR with conventional B-mode USG, there was significantly
 improved in specificity (80.3%) and accuracy (75.1%) with good negative predictive value
 (NPV) (88.7%), despite a slightly lower sensitivity (49.1%).
Conclusion:
The combination of E I /B and SR can improve the specificity and accuracy with insignificant
 change of the high NPV. Incorporating E I /B and SR can be a useful and non-invasive
 additional method to improve the diagnostic performance of conventional B-mode USG,
 potentially reducing the need for unnecessary biopsy of benign solid BI-RADS 4 lesions.

Title: CONTRAST ENHANCED MAMMOGRAPHY (CEM) IN THE ASSESSMENT OF BREAST LESIONS IN A DIAGNOSTIC SETTING
Authors: Thum Wan Qin 1, Kartini Rahmat 1, Wong Yee Voon1, Leong Wai Ling1 , Faizatul Izza Rozalli 1, Farhana Fadzli 2 , Jeannie Wong Hsiu Ding1.
Affiliations: Universiti Malaya Medical Centre (1) Picasso Medical Centre (2)
Keywords: Breast cancer; contrast-enhanced mammography; digital breast tomosynthesis; diagnostic accuracy.
Background: In conventional mammography, malignant lesions may be obscured by overlapping fibroglandular parenchyma due to similar radiodensities. While digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) provides thin cross-sectional slices to reduce tissue overlap, contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) exploits tumour neoangiogenesis to enhance lesion conspicuity. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic efficacy of CEM compared with DBT in differentiating benign from malignant breast lesions using histopathological examination (HPE) as the reference standard, and to identify qualitative CEM enhancement features predictive of malignancy.
Materials & Methods: Materials and Methods: Patients scheduled for core needle biopsy or with available HPE results were prospectively recruited. CEM and DBT images were evaluated 4 weeks apart by two breast radiologists using a consensus reading model, blinded to HPE results and prior imaging reports. Chi-square tests and logistic regression analysis were performed to identify significant CEM predictors of malignancy.
Results: Results: A total of 91 patients with 138 identified breast lesions were enrolled. Of these, 129 lesions were histopathologically verified (72 [52.2%] malignant and 57 [41.3%] benign). The remaining 9 lesions (6.5%) demonstrated mammographic stability over a 2-year active surveillance period and were classified as benign for final analysis. CEM demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity than DBT (97.2% vs. 88.9%, p = 0.03), while specificity was comparable between modalities (78.8% vs. 74.2%, p = 0.62). CEM achieved a positive predictive value (PPV) of 83.3% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 96.3%, compared to a PPV of 79.0% and an NPV of 86.0% for DBT. Irregular shape, non-circumscribed margins, high conspicuity, and a heterogeneous enhancement pattern were key CEM predictors of malignancy, producing complete separation and significantly high odds ratios.
Conclusion: CEM demonstrates superior overall diagnostic performance compared to DBT in the detection and characterization of breast lesions. By providing both anatomical and functional vascular data, CEM serves as a highly accurate modality for evaluating breast malignancies and represents a practical alternativeâ€”particularly in resource-limited settings.
